He also has sensorineural deafness and requires a hearing aid. His current medication includes basal-bolus insulin regime consisting of insulin aspart tds and insulin glargine together with desmopressin bd. He has an average self-monitored glucose profile of 7.6 mmol/L. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents to the follow up annual diabetes clinic. He has had vomiting and abdominal bloating for a few months. He denies any weight loss or diarrhoea. He has a past medical history of hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and gastroesophageal reflux. His diabetes-related complications are retinopathy and nephropathy. He is a smoker with a 20-pack year history. He is taking lansoprazole, aspirin, ramipril, atenolol and simvastatin. On examination, he has central obesity and his general and systemic examination are unremarkable. About 6 months ago his HbA1C was 11.4%. He undergoes gastric motility testing which shows gastroparesis. Which of the following antiemetics has the strongest evidence for effectiveness for this condition?

His diabetes-related complications are retinopathy and nephropathy. He is a smoker with a 20-pack year history. He is taking lansoprazole, aspirin, ramipril, atenolol and simvastatin. On examination, he has central obesity and his general and systemic examination are unremarkable. About 6 months ago his HbA1C was 11.4%. He undergoes gastric motility testing which shows gastroparesis. Which of the following antiemetics has the strongest evidence for effectiveness for this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Domperidone: For adults with type 2 diabetes who have vomiting caused by gastroparesis, there is no strong evidence that any available antiemetic therapy is effective. Yet some people do benefit from domperidone, erythromycin or metoclopramide. Incorrect Options: Option A - Cyclizine: Cyclizine is an antihistamine used to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting. It is not typically used as a primary treatment for gastroparesis. Option C - Erythromycin: Erythromycin, an antibiotic, is sometimes used in gastroparesis due to its prokinetic effect on the stomach muscles. However, its use can be limited by concerns about antibiotic resistance and potential side effects. Option D - Metoclopramide: Metoclopramide is another prokinetic agent used to treat gastroparesis. While it is effective for some individuals, it has been associated with neurological side effects and is often considered as a second-line option due to safety concerns. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 26-year-old lady has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, according to her diagnosis. Which of the following therapies has the best chance of easing her symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old lady has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, according to her diagnosis. Which of the following therapies has the best chance of easing her symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Thiazide diuretics: A deficiency in the kidney's response to vasopressin underlies nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which results in an inability to concentrate urine and an increase in urine output. Because thiazide diuretics paradoxically limit urine production by reducing the volume of fluid reaching the distal tubules, which improves vasopressin's effects, they are the most effective treatment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Vasopressin analogues: Vasopressin analogues are unsuccessful in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, where the kidneys cannot respond to vasopressin because these drugs imitate the effects of vasopressin. Option C - Loop diuretics: Loop diuretics are inappropriate because they generate diuresis, which is harmful in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and act on the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Option D - Water deprivation: Water restriction is inappropriate since it can be challenging to execute and may induce electrolyte imbalances and dehydration. Although water restriction is not the primary treatment for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, it may be required in rare circumstances. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic for evaluation of recurrent episodes of lethargy, sweating and syncope, which improve by consuming fruit juice. He also reports a family history of multiple endocrine tumours. Laboratory investigations reveal low blood glucose levels with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide levels. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic for evaluation of recurrent episodes of lethargy, sweating and syncope, which improve by consuming fruit juice. He also reports a family history of multiple endocrine tumours. Laboratory investigations reveal low blood glucose levels with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide levels. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - MEN 1: This patient's clinical presentation with recurrent episodes of lethargy, sweating and syncope, which improve by consuming fruit juice , suggests recurrent hypoglycemia . The low blood glucose levels with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide levels suggest the presence of an insulinoma , and a family history of multiple endocrine tumours is consistent with multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome (MEN 1) . Multiple endocrine neoplasias should be considered in patients with solitary tumours with a family history of other endocrine tumours (as seen in this patient). MEN 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder that predisposes individuals to develop tumours in multiple endocrine glands, including Pituitary tumours (Growth hormone) Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours : Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, VIPomas, glucagonomas. Parathyroid adenomas MEN 1 syndrome is caused by a mutation in the MEN1 tumour suppressor gene located on chromosome 11. Incorrect Options: Option A - Insulinoma: Insulinoma is a type of tumour that originates from the beta cells of the pancreas , which can lead to excessive insulin production . It is characterised by recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia that improve on normalisation of blood glucose and elevated C-peptide levels . However, multiple endocrine neoplasias should be considered in patients with insulinoma with a family history of other endocrine tumours. Option C - MEN 2A: MEN 2A is associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism . A mutation in the RET proto-oncogene causes it. However, it is not associated with p ancreatic endocrine tumours like insulinoma. The presence of recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia in this patient that improve on normalisation of blood glucose and elevated C-peptide levels are consistent with insulinoma, ruling out the possibility of MEN 2A in this patient. Option D - MEN 2B: Although MEN 2B is also an autosomal dominant disorder that affects the endocrine system, it is associated with medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and neuromas of the mucosa. It is also associated with a marfanoid habitus, i.e., Skeletal abnormalities such as increased arm span, pectus excavatum, scoliosis, weak joints etc. However, this patient's symptoms of recurrent hypoglycemia are not typically seen in MEN 2B. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 42-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department complaining of constipation and depressive mode for the last two months. He also reports generalised weakness. His general physical, as well as systemic examinations, are unremarkable. Baseline investigations, including thyroid profile, are requested. All the pathology results are within normal limits apart from thyroid stimulating hormone levels greater than 10mU/L and normal circulating T4 levels. His TSH was greater than 10mU/L four months back. What would be the management of the disorder?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department complaining of constipation and depressive mode for the last two months. He also reports generalised weakness. His general physical, as well as systemic examinations, are unremarkable. Baseline investigations, including thyroid profile, are requested. All the pathology results are within normal limits apart from thyroid stimulating hormone levels greater than 10mU/L and normal circulating T4 levels. His TSH was greater than 10mU/L four months back. What would be the management of the disorder?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Start levothyroxine: The patient has complaints of constipation and generalised weakness . He has a TSH level of greater than 10mU/L on two separate occasions. However, his T4 levels are within normal limits . It indicates a diagnosis of sub-clinical hypothyroidism . And management at this stage includes the administration of levothyroxine. Elevated blood thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration in the presence of normal serum-free thyroxine is the biochemical definition of subclinical hypothyroidism (T4). TSH is elevated in sub-clinical hypothyroidism, but T3 and T4 levels are normal , with no overt symptoms. The possibility of overt hypothyroidism exists. It can convert into hypothyroidism is 2%-5% per year. It is more prevalent in men . The presence of thyroid autoantibodies increases the risk. Management : Not every patient needs to be treated. Levothyroxine is administered if the TSH value is greater than 10 mU/L twice, three months apart, and the free thyroxine level is within the normal range. If the patient is younger than 65 years old, the TSH level is between 5.5 and 10mU/L, and the free thyroxine level is within the normal range, consider giving levothyroxine a 6-month trial. The trial is given if the level of TSH is 5.5 - 10mU/L on two separate occasions three months apart or if there are symptoms of hypothyroidism. In patients above 80 years, the watch-and-wait strategy is indicated. If patients are asymptomatic, observe and repeat thyroid function in 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option B - A six-month trial of levothyroxine: If the level of TSH is between 5.5 - 10mU/L and the free thyroxine level is within the normal range. If the patient is less than 65 years of age , consider offering a 6-month trial of levothyroxine. The patient mentioned above is 42 years of age and has a TSH level greater than 10mU/L, so levothyroxine should be started. Option C - Watch and wait strategy: In patients above 80 years, the watch-and-wait strategy is indicated. The patient above is 42 years, so thyroxine replacement therapy is indicated. Option D - Repeat thyroid profile in 6 months: If the patient is asymptomatic and has TSH of more than 10mU/L , then the thyroid profile must be repeated in 6 months. The patient mentioned above has had high TSH twice , so levothyroxine must be given. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the office due to breast and pubic hair development seven months ago. The patient has no other symptoms. The Tanner stage of pubic hair is 3, and the Tanner stage of breasts is 3. Her bone age is 8. Basil's LH level is high. Which of the following should be the next step in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the office due to breast and pubic hair development seven months ago. The patient has no other symptoms. The Tanner stage of pubic hair is 3, and the Tanner stage of breasts is 3. Her bone age is 8. Basil's LH level is high. Which of the following should be the next step in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - MRI brain: Patients with early secondary sexual development have precocious puberty. The definition of precocious puberty is the development of secondary sexual characteristics in girls aged less than 8 years and boys aged less than 9 years . It is due to premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Whenever a child comes with precocious puberty, then always find the bone age. If the patient has advanced bone age with high Basil LH, it is central precocious puberty. A GnRH stimulation test should be done if the patient has advanced bone age with low basil LH. On laboratory results, if low LH, then it is peripheral precocious puberty. If high LH, then it is central precocious puberty. If normal bone age is associated with isolated breast development, it is premature thelarche. If normal bone age is associated with isolated pubic hair development, it is premature adrenarche. So, in this case, if the patient has advanced bone age with high Basil LH , then it is most likely Central precocious puberty, so that's why an MRI of the brain should be done to identify a hypothalamic or pituitary tumour. Incorrect Options: Option A - CT scan of adrenal: Adrenal CT scan is done to evaluate the adrenal tumours with low LH and FSH levels. Option B - Dexamethasone suppression test: Dexamethasone suppression test is used to diagnose Cushing syndrome. It presents with acne, a moon-shaped red face, hypertension and skin atrophy. Option C - Karyotyping: Karyotyping is not indicated in precocious puberty. It is used usually to detect abnormalities, for example, Klinefelter syndrome and Turner syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is true concerning the estimation of nutritional needs in a critically ill patient?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true concerning the estimation of nutritional needs in a critically ill patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Albumin and prealbumin are the best measures of nutritional status in critically ill patients

options.label: B
options.text: Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients

options.label: C
options.text: Healthy patients have a daily protein requirement of 1.8 g/kg/day actual body weight

options.label: D
options.text: The absence of bowel sounds is a contraindication to enteral feeding

questions.answerText: Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients: Although a short period of nutritional deprivation may be tolerated, physiologic function and nutritional status are affected by significant deprivation over 1-2 weeks. Factors that influence the need for nutritional supplementation include pre-illness status and severity and duration of metabolic stress. In critically ill patients, nutritional support should be initiated relatively as early as 24-48 hours after admission, as it may improve outcomes. If oral intake cannot maintain adequate nutritional intake, enteral or intravenous routes should be considered. Enteral nutrition is preferable when it is tolerated. Patients who will require 7 days or more of nutrition support should be considered for parenteral nutrition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Albumin and prealbumin are the best measures of nutritional status in critically ill patients: Albumin and prealbumin are acute phase reactants and may be falsely elevated in critically ill patients. Option C - Healthy patients have a daily protein requirement of 1.8 g/kg/day actual body weight : The protein requirement for a healthy patient is 0.8 g/kg/day actual body weight. Option D - The absence of bowel sounds is a contraindication to enteral feeding : The only contraindication to enteral feeding is high bowel obstruction. Lack of bowel sounds or lack of flatus are not contraindications to enteral feeding. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Following resection of a tumor of the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, what defect would be expected?
questions.stemHtml: Following resection of a tumor of the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, what defect would be expected?

options.label: C
options.text: A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only

options.label: D
options.text: A monocular right superior quadrantanopia in the right eye only

questions.solution: Correct Option B - A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. Incorrect Options: Option A - A homonymous right inferior quadrantanopia: This option is incorrect because the lesion described in the question involves the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe. Lesions in this area would affect the fibers that carry visual information from the superior right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. Option C - A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Monocular field defects are not caused by lesions in the brain but rather by abnormalities in the eye itself or along the optic nerve. The lesion described in the question is located in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, which is a cerebral region. Therefore, monocular field defects would not be expected. Option D - A monocular right superior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Similar to option C, monocular field defects are not caused by cerebral lesions. A lesion in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe would not result in a monocular field defect in the right eye. Option E - A left afferent pupillary defect: Afferent pupillary defects (also known as a Marcus Gunn pupil) are typically caused by lesions affecting the optic nerve or severe retinal disease in the eye. The lesion described in the question is not located along the optic nerve, and it would not cause an afferent pupillary defect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Renal failure: The adverse effect of acyclovir with the greatest morbidity is crystal-induced nephrotoxicity due to crystallization of the drug within the nephron. Acyclovir has low solubility in urine and therefore it is very important to ensure that patients are not intravascularly depleted as this complication of acyclovir therapy is much higher in patients that are volume contracted. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thrombocytopenia: Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count, which can result in an increased risk of bleeding. Acyclovir is not typically associated with thrombocytopenia as an adverse effect. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require close monitoring specifically for this drug. Option B - Liver Failure: Liver failure involves the severe impairment of liver function. Acyclovir is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, and significant liver toxicity is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy. While liver function tests might be monitored in some cases, liver failure is not a typical concern with acyclovir use. Option D - Pancytopenia : Pancytopenia refers to a decrease in all three major blood cell types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Acyclovir is not typically associated with pancytopenia. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require specific monitoring for this drug. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following presentations of multiple sclerosis (MS) affects men and women at similar rates?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following presentations of multiple sclerosis (MS) affects men and women at similar rates?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Primary-progressive MS: Unlike the relapsing-remitting and secondary progressive forms, which preferentially affect women, primary progressive MS (PPMS) seems to affect men and women equally. PPMS is characterized by a progressive disease course from onset. Patients may have relapses but there is continued disease progression between relapses. Approximately 10-15% of patients with multiple sclerosis present with the primary-progressive form. Incorrect Options: Option B - Relapsing-Remitting MS: Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) is characterized by episodes of neurological symptoms (relapses) followed by periods of partial or complete recovery (remission). RRMS is more common in women than in men. The ratio of women to men with RRMS is generally higher, with estimates ranging from 2:1 to 3:1. Option C - Secondary Progressive MS: Secondary progressive MS (SPMS) is a phase of MS that follows relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS). It involves a progressive worsening of neurological symptoms without the distinct relapses and remissions seen in RRMS. The risk of SPMS is higher in individuals with RRMS who have had the disease for a longer period of time. Like RRMS, SPMS is also more common in women than in men. Option D - All of the Above: This option is incorrect because both relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) and secondary progressive MS (SPMS) are more common in women than in men. Therefore, neither RRMS nor SPMS affects men and women at similar rates. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Everolimus is approved for, and has demonstrated efficacy in treating, which type of tumor?
questions.stemHtml: Everolimus is approved for, and has demonstrated efficacy in treating, which type of tumor?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma: Everolimus has been approved as a targeted therapy for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs), a benign tumor that can nonetheless grow rapidly or hemorrhage, causing neurological complications. Incorrect Options: Option A - Optic Glioma : Optic gliomas are tumors that develop in or around the optic nerve, often associated with a condition called neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Everolimus is not typically used to treat optic gliomas, and there is limited evidence supporting its efficacy in this context. Option B - Cortical Tuber : Cortical tubers are a characteristic feature of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), a genetic disorder that causes non-cancerous tumors to develop in various organs, including the brain. While everolimus is used to treat certain manifestations of TSC, such as subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs), it is not a primary treatment for cortical tubers. Cortical tubers are congenital lesions that consist of dysplastic neurons and astrocytes. These dysplasias are present at birth and are therefore less responsive to treatments like everolimus (though there may be changes in the astrocytes over time that could be modifiable by treatment). Option C - Brainstem Glioma: Brainstem gliomas are tumors that arise in the brainstem, which controls many vital functions. Everolimus is not a standard treatment for brainstem gliomas, and its use in this context has not been well established. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B
options.text: Sensory ataxia neuropathy, dysarthria, limb girdle paresis

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Cardiac conduction defects, pigmentary retinopathy, and disease onset before age 20
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cardiac conduction defects, pigmentary retinopathy, and disease onset before age 20 : While there is considerable overlap in the features of mitochondrial cytopathies that present with CPEO, distinct differences in the hallmark features exist. All of these answer choices reflect the features of a syndrome that either always or sometimes present with CPEO. questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman attends the rheumatology outpatient department for a routine follow up. She is a known case of systemic lupus erythematosus of 2 years. She is on hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) 200 mg, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) 2 gm and prednisolone 5 mg per day for her lupus nephritis (LN) class III. She is asymptomatic at present. Her proteinuria remained < 0.5 gm per 24 hours in the last 6 months with normal renal function. She is planning for pregnancy and has sought your advice on further management of her medications. What should you advise regarding her further management?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Continue the patient on HCQ and prednisolone but MMF should be switched to azathioprine at least 3 months prior to conception: This patient should be advised on continuing with HCQ and prednisolone but she should be switched from MMF to azathioprine (AZA) at least 3 months prior to conception. Recent British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) and British Health Professionals in Rheumatology (BHPR) guidelines on prescribing drugs during pregnancy and breastfeeding recommend that HCQ should be continued during pregnancy and that prednisolone is also compatible with each trimester of pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Continue the patient on HCQ and prednisolone but MMF should be switched to azathioprine at least 6 weeks prior to conception: While transitioning from MMF to azathioprine is a step in the right direction, the timing mentioned (at least 6 weeks prior to conception) might not provide sufficient time for azathioprine to fully take effect and replace MMF. Azathioprine is a safer option during pregnancy compared to MMF, but a longer transition period is usually recommended to ensure the patient's condition remains stable and her lupus nephritis is well managed before she conceives. Option C - Continue the patient on HCQ and MMF but prednisolone should be stopped 6 weeks before planned pregnancy: Prednisolone is often continued during pregnancy in cases of lupus nephritis to prevent disease flares and maintain disease control. Abruptly stopping prednisolone can increase the risk of lupus flares, which can have negative effects on both the patient's health and pregnancy outcomes. Option D - Continue the patient on MMF and prednisolone but HCQ should be stopped 6 weeks before planned pregnancy: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is considered safe for use during pregnancy and is often recommended to be continued throughout pregnancy in patients with lupus. HCQ can help manage disease activity and reduce the risk of lupus flares. Stopping HCQ abruptly before conception might not be necessary and can potentially lead to disease exacerbation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Gustatory stimulants: Oral dryness in patients with Sjogren’s syndrome is classified into mild, moderate, and severe. In patients with mild oral dryness, non-pharmacological modalities, like gustatory stimulants (sugar-free candies, lozenges, xylitol) or mechanical stimulants (sugar-free chewing gum), can be tried. In patients with moderate oral dryness, salivary stimulants like muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine and cevimeline) may be tried. While it can be effective in managing dry mouth symptoms, it's not the first-line treatment option and may be considered when other approaches are not providing sufficient relief. Option C- Hydroxychloroquine: Is an antimalarial medication that is also used as an immunomodulatory agent in various autoimmune diseases, including Sjögren's syndrome. It can help manage certain symptoms of Sjögren's, such as joint pain and fatigue, but it might not be the primary choice for treating oral dryness. Option D- Pilocarpine: Is another medication used to increase saliva production in individuals with dry mouth associated with Sjögren's syndrome. The periorbital heliotrope rash can be associated with quite marked oedema and the Gottron's papules on the extensor surfaces can ulcerate. The myopathy is proximal and inflammatory arthritis occurs in a third of cases. Extra-articular calcification can occur and flexion contractures can be marked leading to serious disability. While it can cause joint symptoms, such as arthritis, the presence of periorbital oedema, ulcerated rash, and periungual telangiectasia in this case is more suggestive of juvenile dermatomyositis. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Amantidine: Prevention of influenza virus in children under the age of 6 months consists of vaccinating caretakers and close contacts, good hand hygiene, and restricting sick contacts. questions.answerText: The first hour of recognition of septic shock
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The first hour of recognition of septic shock: The administration of effective intravenous antimicrobials within the first hour of recognition of septic shock (grade 1B) and severe sepsis without septic shock should be the goal of therapy. Although most evidence supports the prompt administration of antibiotics following the recognition of severe sepsis and septic shock, the feasibility with which clinicians may achieve this ideal state has not been scientifically evaluated. Moreover, initial empiric anti-infective therapy should include 1 or more drugs that have activity against all likely pathogens (bacterial and/or fungal or viral) and that penetrate in adequate concentrations into the tissues presumed to be the source of sepsis. The antimicrobial regimen should be reassessed daily for potential de-escalation to prevent the development of resistance, reduce toxicity, and reduce costs. It is suggested to use low procalcitonin levels or similar biomarkers to aid the discontinuation of empiric antibiotics in patients who appeared septic but had no subsequent evidence of infection. Incorrect Options: Option B - First 2 hours of recognition of septic shock: Although the feasibility of a one-hour target for initiating antibiotics has not been tested, the rationale for using it is based on observational studies that show poor outcomes with delayed (even beyond one hour), inadequately dosed, or inappropriate (ie, treatment with antibiotics to which the pathogen was later shown to be in vitro resistant) antimicrobial therapy. Option C - First 6 hours of recognition of septic shock: The administration of effective intravenous antimicrobials within the first hour of recognition of septic shock (grade 1B) and severe sepsis without septic shock should be the goal of therapy. Option D - Varied depending on the causative organism suspected: The duration of treatment initiation doesn’t depend on the causative organism. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with type 2 diabetes and renal failure was admitted to the hospital following several days of shortness of breath, cough, and fever concerning pneumonia. He was empirically started on vancomycin, cefepime, azithromycin, and fluconazole. All medications were appropriately administered. On day 2 of admission, despite the improvement of the patient's leukocytosis and a near resolution of his fever, he started becoming progressively more confused and exhibited facial myoclonus. His electrolytes, liver enzymes, and ammonia levels were normal. Renal function is at his baseline. An MRI of the brain shows no abnormalities. CSF studies are normal. An EEG rules out nonconvulsive status epilepticus but shows some triphasic sharp waves. After stopping an antibiotic, within 24-48 hours the patient’s mental status rapidly improves and returns to baseline. Another antibiotic is chosen to complete the therapy. Which medication was stopped?

questions.stem: A 15-year-old African American boy presented to the clinic after an episode of gross hematuria. He has a history of excessive urination and wakes 2-3 times at night for urination. His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following: Specific gravity 1.005 Protein None Blood Moderate Red blood cells Many/hpf Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 15-year-old African American boy presented to the clinic after an episode of gross hematuria. He has a history of excessive urination and wakes 2-3 times at night for urination. His physical examination shows no abnormalities. His mother died of a stroke when he was 2 years of age. Urinalysis show’s following:
			Specific gravity
			1.005
			Protein
			None
			Blood
			Moderate
			Red blood cells
			Many/hpf
Which part of the kidney is affected in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Renal papillae This patient presents with gross hematuria with complaints of polyuria with a low urine specific gravity consistent with hyposthenuria and the inability of the kidneys to concentrate urine, a feature of sickle cell disease. His family history is significant for early-onset stroke, which can be a severe complication of sickle cell disease (SCD) due to cerebrovascular occlusion from sickling. However, he has no other symptoms. Therefore, sickle cell trait (SCT) is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Sickle cell trait is a benign condition associated with hemoglobin AS that is more common in Africa, the Middle East, and Mediterranean countries and African American and Hispanic individuals. Hyposthenuria is common in patients with SCD and may also develop in those with SCT. In response to hypoxic, hyperosmolar conditions of the renal medulla, red blood cells sickle in the vasa recta, impairing free water reabsorption and countercurrent exchange. Patients typically have polyuria and nocturia despite fluid restriction. Urine osmolality is low; however, normal serum sodium is maintained due to intact antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Urinary diluting capacity is also intact as it is a function of the superficial loop of Henle, which is not supplied by the vasa recta. Non-glomerular hematuria is characterized by gross hematuria with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) but without significant proteinuria. Etiologies include: Cancer (e.g. renal cell, prostate) Infections (e.g. cystitis) Polycystic kidney disease Nephrolithiasis Papillary necrosis Gross hematuria can be from: Bladder (e.g. cystitis. cancer) Renal (e.g. glomerulonephritis) Ureteral pathology (e.g. nephrolithiasis) Prostate pathology (e.g. benign prostatic hyperplasia) This patient's gross hematuria and urinalysis with normal-appearing red blood cells (RBCs) suggest an extra-glomerular etiology. Painless hematuria is likely due to renal papillary ischemia or necrosis. The relatively low local partial pressure of oxygen in the vasa recta predisposes the affected red blood cells to sickle. Papillary necrosis can occur with massive hematuria, but the episodes are usually mild and resolve spontaneously. The urinalysis usually shows normal-appearing RBCs. It may be associated with sickle cell disease/trait. Other renal complications include: Hyposthenuria; inability to concentrate the urine (vasa recta damage with an inability to maintain concentrated medullary gradient) Distal renal tubular acidosis (tubular damage with impaired H+ secretion). Incorrect options: Option B: Renal interstitium The renal interstitium refers to the connective tissue and extracellular matrix that comprise the space between the renal tubules and blood vessels in the kidney. The interstitium plays an important role in regulating renal function by providing support and structural organization for the various components of the kidney. One of the primary functions of the renal interstitium is to maintain the integrity of the renal tubules and blood vessels. The interstitium contains collagen fibers and other extracellular matrix components that support and help maintain the structural integrity of the kidney. The interstitium also contains various cells, including fibroblasts and macrophages, involved in tissue repair and immune defense. The interstitium is also important for regulating fluid and electrolyte balance in the kidney. The interstitial fluid communicates with the blood and the tubular fluid, exchanging ions and solutes between these compartments. The interstitium is also involved in the production and secretion of various hormones and growth factors that regulate renal function. Renal tumors or malignancies (e.g., renal cell cancer) involving the interstitium can present as non-glomerular hematuria. However, isosthenuria would not be typically seen with this condition. Option C: Glomerulus The glomerulus is a specialized structure in the kidney that plays a critical role in blood filtration and urine production. It is a small, spherical structure composed of a network of capillaries, known as glomerular capillaries, that is surrounded by a layer of specialized cells called podocytes. The glomerular capillaries are highly permeable, allowing water and small solutes to pass through the Bowman's capsule, the first part of the renal tubule. The podocytes, which have unique finger-like projections called foot processes, form a barrier that helps to regulate the passage of larger molecules, such as proteins, into the Bowman's capsule. Blood filtration in the glomerulus is regulated by complex interactions between the podocytes, mesangial cells, and the blood vessels that supply the glomerulus. These interactions help to maintain the proper balance of fluid and solutes in the body while preventing the loss of important molecules such as proteins. Glomerular hematuria refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine that originate from the glomerulus in the kidney. This condition can be caused by several different physiological factors, which are as follows: Damage to the glomerular capillaries, e.g. glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and vasculitis. Abnormalities in the structure or function of the glomerular filtration barrier, e.g. Alport syndrome. Abnormalities in platelet function or coagulation, e.g. thrombotic microangiopathy. Diseases of the glomerulus cause microscopic hematuria, though gross hematuria may be present in some cases. It is usually due to glomerulonephritis (GN or basement membrane disease. Symptoms are usually absent or nonspecific (e.g., low back pain), and patients may present after developing features of the nephritic syndrome (e.g., hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, elevated creatinine). Urinalysis usually shows proteinuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts. Option D: Renal Tubules Renal tubules are the microscopic tubes in the kidney that filter blood and produce urine. They are located in the nephrons, the kidney's functional units. The renal tubules comprise several distinct segments, each with a unique structure and function. Hematuria caused by the renal tubules, also known as tubular hematuria, refers to the presence of red blood cells in the urine originating from the kidney tubules. Causes of tubular hematuria include: Damage to the renal tubules, e.g. interstitial nephritis, polycystic kidney disease, and certain medications. Kidney stones. Bleeding disorders, such as von Willebrand disease or thrombocytopenia. Acute tubular necrosis is characterized by acute azotemia following a hypotensive or nephrotoxic injury. Patients may have dark or cola-coloured urine, but significant hematuria is uncommon. Tubulointerstitial nephritis causes microscopic hematuria associated with elevated creatinine and variable proteinuria. It is most commonly due to certain medications, including antibiotics, NSAIDs, and diuretics. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of fatigue, weakness, and muscle cramps for the past few days. She also reports experiencing frequent headaches and episodes of palpitations. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, which has been poorly controlled despite being on medication. On physical examination, the patient appears to be fatigued and dehydrated. His blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, and his heart rate is 110 beats per minute. Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia (serum potassium level of 2.8 mEq/L), and an elevated serum aldosterone level of 50 ng/dL (normal range 5-30 ng/dL). Which of the following could be found in the labs of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of fatigue, weakness, and muscle cramps for the past few days. She also reports experiencing frequent headaches and episodes of palpitations. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, which has been poorly controlled despite being on medication. On physical examination, the patient appears to be fatigued and dehydrated. His blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, and his heart rate is 110 beats per minute. Laboratory investigations show hypokalemia (serum potassium level of 2.8 mEq/L), and an elevated serum aldosterone level of 50 ng/dL (normal range 5-30 ng/dL). Which of the following could be found in the labs of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Decreased serum H+ levels: In this clinical scenario, the patient's history of poorly controlled hypertension, hypokalemia , and elevated serum aldosterone levels suggest a diagnosis of hyperaldosteronism . Hyperaldosteronism leads to increased renal potassium excretion, resulting in hypokalemia. This hypokalemia, in turn, increases hydrogen ion secretion in the distal renal tubules , leading to metabolic alkalosis, as seen in this patient with a high serum bicarbonate level and an alkaline arterial blood pH. Incorrect Options: Option B- Increased serum chloride levels: It is incorrect, as hyperaldosteronism may cause a decrease in serum chloride levels due to increased bicarbonate reabsorption in the kidneys. Option C- Decreased serum sodium levels: It is also incorrect, as serum sodium levels may increase or remain normal ( due to the aldosterone escape mechanism) but not decreased Option D- Increased serum calcium levels: It is not directly affected by hyperaldosteronism-induced metabolic alkalosis . @Neet_pg_bot

Option C - Right coronary artery: The right coronary artery (RCA) mainly supplies the SA node and the inferior aspect of the heart. She reports a history of palpitations on exertion in the past but never to this extent. On examination, her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and her heart rate is 220/min with a regular rhythm. questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with palpitations and shortness of breath started a few minutes ago at a concert. She reports a history of palpitations on exertion in the past but never to this extent. On examination, her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and her heart rate is 220/min with a regular rhythm. His ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia with a regular rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT): The patient's symptoms and ECG findings are consistent with the diagnosis of AVRT, a type of supraventricular tachycardia caused by an abnormal accessory pathway between the atria and ventricles. During AVRT, there is a re-entry circuit between the AV node and the accessory pathway, causing a narrow complex tachycardia with a regular rhythm. The delta wave on the ECG represents the premature activation of the ventricles via the accessory pathway, resulting in a shortened PR interval. Symptoms: The patient's palpitations and shortness of breath are typical of the hemodynamic effects of tachycardia. Management: The initial management of AVRT is usually to attempt to terminate the tachycardia using vagal manoeuvres or pharmacologic agents that block conduction through the accessory pathway. Carotid sinus pressure and intravenous adenosine are both effective in terminating AVRT in many cases. If the patient remains symptomatic despite these interventions, electrical cardioversion may be necessary. Long-term management of AVRT may involve catheter ablation of the accessory pathway, particularly in patients with frequent or symptomatic episodes. Incorrect Options: Option A- Sinus tachycardia: Sinus tachycardia is an arrhythmia where the heart beats faster than normal. It originates from the sinus node, the natural pacemaker of the heart The heart rate is usually between 100-130 beats per minute but can go up to 220 in extreme cases The ECG shows a regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes and upright P waves preceding each QRS complex Since this patient has tachycardia associated with PR shortening and QRS widening with the appearance of a delta wave. This is certainly not sinus tachycardia. Option B- Atrial flutter: Atrial flutter is an abnormal heart rhythm in the upper chambers of the heart (atria). It creates a circular movement in the right atrium, seen as a saw-tooth pattern on ECG. Heart rate is usually around 150 bpm but can be as high as 300 bpm. Atrial flutter can cause a 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 block of impulses to the lower chambers (ventricles), leading to a slower heart rate. Option C- Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT): Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia: AVNRT is a fast and regular heart rhythm caused by a re-entry circuit in the heart's electrical system. It usually occurs in people without heart disease and can cause chest discomfort, lightheadedness, and breathlessness. Treatment options include maneuvers like carotid sinus pressure or Valsalva, medications like adenosine or verapamil, and in severe cases, DC cardioversion. Which one of the following is the most common anatomical area of the heart where the reentry tract for PSVT is usually present?

He was diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. His parents want to know all possible treatment options. An electrophysiologist explains that catheter ablation of the reentry tract is the most definitive treatment. Which one of the following is the most common anatomical area of the heart where the reentry tract for PSVT is usually present?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - AV node: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) is a type of heart arrhythmia that is characterized by an abnormally fast heart rate that starts and stops suddenly. The abnormal connection between the top and bottom chambers of the heart in PSVT is often caused by a reentry tract, which is an abnormal electrical pathway in the heart. This reentry tract is mostly located at the AV node and can create a loop of electrical signals that travel from the atria to the ventricles and back again, overwhelming the AV node and causing rapid and irregular heartbeats . In some cases, catheter ablation can be used to destroy the reentry tract and restore normal electrical conduction in the heart. Catheter ablation is a procedure in which a thin, flexible tube (catheter) is inserted into a blood vessel and guided to the heart. Once in position, the catheter delivers energy (such as radiofrequency or cryotherapy) to the reentry tract to destroy the abnormal pathway and prevent the arrhythmia from occurring. Incorrect Options: Option A - SA node: The SA node is a cluster of specialized cells located in the heart that functions as a natural pacemaker, generating electrical impulses that regulate the heart's rhythm. These impulses travel through the heart's electrical system, causing the atria and ventricles to contract in a synchronized way , resulting in an efficient heartbeat. SA node is the origin of the cardiac impulse and can not act as a reentry point. Option C - Bundle of His: The Bundle of His, also known as the AV bundle, is a group of specialized cells within the heart's electrical conduction system. Its function is to carry electrical signals from the AV node to the ventricles , causing them to contract and pump blood out of the heart. It is located at the upper part of the ventricular septum and is divided into two main branches, the left and right bundle branches. It is an important part of the normal electrical conduction system of the heart, but it is not typically involved in the reentry pathway that causes paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). Option D - Purkinje fibers: Purkinje fibers are situated in the ventricular walls and extend from the Bundle of His and its branches. Purkinje fibers have a lower threshold for depolarization compared to other cardiac muscle fibers, which means that they are more easily stimulated by electrical impulses. @Neet_pg_bot

Physical examination reveals a barrel-shaped chest and bilateral wheezing on auscultation. There is 2+ pitting oedema and dilated superficial veins over both lower legs. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Abnormal pulmonary artery systolic pressure: This patient’s smoking history, clinical features, and physical examination suggest chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary hypertension is a medical condition with abnormally elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary vessels. Pulmonary hypertension has five groups: Group 1: Pulmonary arterial hypertensio n: The cause of pulmonary arterial hypertension in most cases is unknown. It is also called idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. Group 2: Pulmonary hypertension caused by left-sided heart dis orders: It is caused by mitral valve or aortic valve disease. Left-ventricular failure can also lead to pulmonary hypertension. Group 3: Pulmonary hypertension caused by lung dis orders: This group included patients who develop pulmonary hypertension because of disorders that affect the respiratory system, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), fibrosis of lung parenchyma, and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Group 4: Pulmonary hypertension caused by thrombosis: This group included patients who develop pulmonary hypertension due to blood clots in pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary emboli) or other thrombotic disorders. Group 5: Pulmonary hypertension caused by other medical disorders: This group included patients who develop pulmonary hypertension due to kidney disorders, metabolic disorders, malignancy pressing against the pulmonary arteries, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and blood disorders such as polycythemia and thrombocythemia. Increasing age elevates the risk of pulmonary hypertension. However, idiopathic pulmonary hypertension is more common in women in their thirties. Other risk factors include: Family history of pulmonary hypertension Obesity Blood clotting diseases or family history of pulmonary embolism Asbestos Exposure Congenital heart disorders Residing at a high elevation Use of certain medicines like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or illicit drugs like cocaine or methamphetamine. Initial symptoms of pulmonary hypertension include breathing difficulty and tiredness. Other symptoms include pain in the chest, generalized weakness, palpitations, and oedema. There are four stages of pulmonary hypertension, depending upon the severity of the symptoms: Class 1: No symptoms Class 2: No symptoms at rest. Dyspnea on strenuous activity. Class 3: No symptoms present at rest. Dyspnea on mild exertion. Class 4: Patient is symptomatic at rest. Diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension is made by taking history, performing a physical examination, and conducting several tests. Chest X-ray: It is conducted to look for lung abnormalities that can lead to pulmonary hypertension. Doppler echocardiography: It can calculate the flow of blood via heart valves. It helps to measure the systolic pulmonary artery pressure. It also helps to check how well the treatment is working. Right heart catheterisation: It is performed to diagnose pulmonary hypertension. The catheter is inserted into the right side of the heart and pulmonary artery to measure blood pressure directly. The catheterisation must show more than 25 mm Hg pulmonary artery systolic pressure. Other tests: There are several other tests that may be conducted to help make the diagnosis, including CT Scan, MRI, Pulmonary function test (PFT), polysomnography, and open lung biopsy.   • Initial symptoms of pulmonary hypertension include breathing difficulty and tiredness.

  • Diagnosis of pulmonary hypertension is made by taking history, performing a physical examination, and conducting several tests.

  • Doppler echocardiography: It can calculate the flow of blood via heart valves. It helps to measure the systolic pulmonary artery pressure. It also helps to check how well the treatment is working.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with worsening pain and swelling in his right groin, which developed after undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) through the right femoral artery. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass in the right groin with surrounding erythema and tenderness. Auscultation of the mass reveals a systolic bruit at the femoral artery puncture site. What is the most likely complication of PCI in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with worsening pain and swelling in his right groin, which developed after undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) through the right femoral artery. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass in the right groin with surrounding erythema and tenderness. Auscultation of the mass reveals a systolic bruit at the femoral artery puncture site. What is the most likely complication of PCI in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Pseudoaneurysm: Pseudoaneurysm formation is a rare but potentially serious vascular complication of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) . It occurs when there is a disruption in the continuity of the vessel wall , resulting in a contained hematoma that communicates with the arterial lumen through a small neck or tract. Pseudoaneurysms can occur at the site of the arterial access or any point along the catheterisation pathway and are most commonly seen after femoral artery access. Symptoms of pseudoaneurysm may include swelling, pain, and a pulsatile mass at the site of the arterial access. Auscultation of the pulsatile mass typically reveals a systolic bruit . In some cases, patients may also experience signs of bleeding, such as hematoma or hypotension. Diagnosis is typically confirmed using Doppler ultrasound, which can identify the characteristic swirling blood flow within the aneurysm sac. If left untreated, pseudoaneurysms can lead to thromboembolism, rupture, or chronic fistula formation. Therefore, timely intervention is important. Management options include conservative observation, ultrasound-guided compression, percutaneous thrombin injection, or surgical repair , depending on the size and location of the aneurysm, the patient's clinical status, and the experience of the treating physician. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hematoma: Hematoma is a common vascular complication after PCI, presenting as localized swelling or bruising without pulsation. Option B - Femoral nerve injury: Femoral nerve injury can occur during vascular access due to the proximity of the nerve to the femoral artery . However, it usually presents with paresthesias and patellar tendon hyporeflexia of the ipsilateral thigh. Option C - Arteriovenous fistula: An arteriovenous fistula is another rare complication that occurs when there is direct communication between the arterial and venous systems, causing the shunting of blood flow . It causes a continuous bruit with a palpable thrill rather than a systolic bruit and does not usually present as a pulsatile mass. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Embolic stroke: Endocarditis is an infection of the heart's inner lining, typically caused by bacterial or fungal organisms. Intravenous drug use is a significant risk factor for developing endocarditis. Staphylococcus aureus is a normal skin flora and can be introduced to the bloodstream during IV abuse. The most common complication of endocarditis is embolic events, which occur in up to 30% of patients with endocarditis. Emboli can cause various problems, including ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attacks, and peripheral embolization. In this case, the patient has several risk factors for endocarditis, including a history of intravenous drug use and a heart murmur. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, confirming the diagnosis of endocarditis. Given the high prevalence of embolic events in patients with endocarditis, an embolic stroke is the most likely complication in this patient. The patient would present with acute neurological deficits, such as hemiparesis, hemiplegia, or aphasia, depending on the location of the embolus. Incorrect Options: Option B- Acute heart failure: Acute heart failure may occur in patients with endocarditis due to damage to the heart valves or myocardium. However, this complication typically occurs later in the disease course and is less common than embolic events. This patient's acute heart failure is less likely based on the acute presentation and lack of significant valvular damage. Option C- Mycotic Aneurysm: Mycotic aneurysm is a rare complication of endocarditis that occurs when an infected embolus lodges in a small arterial branch causing a mushroom shaped dilation of infected vessels and causes an inflammatory reaction, leading to an aneurysm and often involve the middle cerebral artery. This complication typically presents with localized symptoms, such as pain or swelling, depending on the location of the aneurysm. In this patient, the mycotic aneurysm is less likely based on the absence of localized symptoms. Option D- Septic Arthritis: Septic arthritis can occur in patients with endocarditis if an infected embolus lodges in a joint space. This complication typically presents with joint pain, swelling, and limited range of motion. However, septic arthritis is less likely in this patient based on the absence of joint symptoms on examination. @Neet_pg_bot

In a patient who had a previous encounter with a specific pathogen, the immune system's ability to respond more rapidly and effectively upon re-exposure is known as immunological memory. This phenomenon involves both B cells and T cells. Regarding memory B cells, which of the following is the primary mechanism responsible for their formation?
Select the most accurate option that describes the process leading to the formation of memory B cells and their role in immunological memory

options.label: C
options.text: Production of IL10 by T cells

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Sustained binding of CD40-CD40L: Memory B cells are primarily formed through sustained interactions between CD40 molecules on B cells and CD40 ligands (CD40L) on activated T cells. CD40-CD40L interactions are crucial for the germinal center reactions that take place during the immune response. These interactions help B cells receive signals for survival, proliferation, and differentiation into memory B cells and antibody-secreting plasma cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Direct differentiation from centroblast: Memory B cells do not directly differentiate from centroblasts. Centroblasts are activated B cells that undergo somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination in the germinal center of lymph nodes, leading to the generation of high-affinity antibody-secreting plasma cells and memory B cells. Option B - Expression of CD45RO marker: CD45RO is a marker commonly associated with memory T cells, not memory B cells. Memory T cells express different isoforms of the CD45 molecule, and CD45RO is one of them. CD45 is a transmembrane protein involved in T cell receptor signalling. Option C - Production of IL10 by T cells: IL-10 (Interleukin-10) is an immunosuppressive cytokine. While it plays a role in immune regulation, it is not the primary mechanism responsible for the formation of memory B cells. Memory B cell development is influenced by interactions between B cells and T cells, but IL-10 is not the primary factor involved. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome often have bleeding episodes due to the combination of low platelet counts and platelet dysfunction. They also have increased IgE levels, which can contribute to the development of eczema. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP), which plays a crucial role in cytoskeletal organization and immune cell function. questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Proximal convoluted tubule A renal tubular acidosis is a group of diseases that results in the inability of the kidneys to excrete acids out of the blood into the urine. As a result of it, metabolic acidosis results. In Renal tubular acidosis type 2, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved which results in the inability to reabsorb the bicarbonate ions leading to metabolic acidosis. However, the distal tubules are working normally and can acidify the urine. That is why metabolic acidosis is less severe. Hypokalemia is also associated with renal tubular acidosis. Some of the symptoms of renal tubular acidosis type 2 are palpitations, irregular heartbeats, paralysis, and death. In RTA type 2, there are low levels of potassium and bicarbonate. Incorrect options: Option A: Early distal tubule The early distal tubule is affected in renal tubular acidosis type 1, in which there is an inability to excrete acid from the body. It can be inherited from parents or it can be associated with autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus, etc. Renal tubular acidosis type 1 patients are prone to kidney stones. Option B: Capillaries In renal tubular acidosis, capillaries are not the cause of metabolic acidosis. Capillaries surround the nephrons and are involved in providing the blood supply and also reabsorb the molecules so that they can be recirculated in the blood. The obstruction of the capillaries can lead to acute kidney injury. Option D: Collecting duct The collecting duct is the last part of the nephron which reabsorbs the water and electrolytes to concentrate the urine. It also excretes waste materials. The collecting duct is mainly controlled by ADH and aldosterone. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Normal anion gap Renal tubular acidosis is due to the inability of the kidney to either excrete hydrogen ions or reabsorb filtered bicarbonate. There are many types of RTA including type 1 RTA, type 2 RTA, and type 4 RTA. Type 1 RTA is due to the inability of the distal tubule of the nephron to excrete hydrogen ions leading to metabolic acidosis. Causes of RTA include primary causes: familial, and idiopathic. Secondary causes include sickle cell anemia, autoimmune (SLE, Sjogren's), hyperparathyroidism, and Vitamin D intoxication, chronic hepatitis, renal transplantation. Anion Gap is used to find the cause of metabolic acidosis. The normal value of the anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Normal anion gap with metabolic acidosis is due to loss of bicarbonate by the kidney( RTA type 1 and RTA type 2) or gut (Diarrhea). Symptoms include increased respiratory rate, irregular heart rate, muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation, nephrocalcinosis, paralysis, and death. There will be hyperkalemia due to hyperaldosteronism. questions.stem: A 36-year-male presented in the hospital ER with a presenting complaint of lethargy, muscle weakness and pain, abdominal pain and constipation. On examination, heart rate: 98/min, respiratory rate:26/min, B.P:100/70 mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:140 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate:12 bicarbonate. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.23. The anion gap is normal. Urine analysis shows pH:5.2, no cast, no RBCs, no protein. Renal tubular acidosis is suspected. What is the buffering mechanism in the kidney to correct acid-base disturbance in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-male presented in the hospital ER with a presenting complaint of lethargy, muscle weakness and pain, abdominal pain and constipation. On examination, heart rate: 98/min, respiratory rate:26/min, B.P:100/70 mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:140 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate:12 bicarbonate. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.23. The anion gap is normal. Urine analysis shows pH:5.2, no cast, no RBCs, no protein. Renal tubular acidosis is suspected. What is the buffering mechanism in the kidney to correct acid-base disturbance in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Phosphate and ammonia buffer system Buffers in the body resist change in the acid-base balance after the addition of either acid or base. There are many types of buffering systems in the body including bicarbonate buffer, hemoglobin buffer, protein buffer etc. The major buffering mechanism in the kidney is the phosphate buffer system and ammonia buffer system. Phosphate buffer is the first line buffering mechanism in the kidney which is freely filtered as mono hydrogen phosphate and is not completely reabsorbed. Monohydrogen phosphate reacts with excess hydrogen ions excreted by the distal tubule of the nephron and forms dihydrogen phosphate. Ammonia buffer is the second line buffering mechanism of the kidney. This ammonia is derived from glutamine in the kidney. Ammonia reacts with excess hydrogen ions and forms ammonium ions. Hydrogen ions in the urine are in 2 forms, dihydrogen phosphate (titratable acid) and ammonium (non-titratable acid). Incorrect options: Option A: Protein Buffer system Protein acts as a buffer in both cells and plasma. Protein is made up of amino acids(A.A). The exposed amine group of A. A accepts hydrogen ions in acidic conditions. The exposed carboxyl group of A. A releases hydrogen ions when there is alkalosis and helps to cancel out its effect. Proteins are not part of the buffering system of the kidney. Option C: Hemoglobin buffer system The Hemoglobin buffer system is the type of protein buffer system inside the RBCs. Hemoglobin is made up of amino acids. Hemoglobin can release and accept hydrogen ions if the condition is alkalotic and acidotic, respectively. Option D: Bicarbonate buffer system The major buffer system in the blood is the bicarbonate buffer system. Carbon dioxide from tissues is converted in RBCs into bicarbonate via the action of carbonic anhydrase and is released back into the plasma. When excess hydrogen ions enter the body, hydrogen ions get neutralized by reacting with bicarbonate forming carbonic acid which dissociates into water and carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is carried to the lungs and is exhaled. In this way, bicarbonate prevents change in the pH of the blood. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Defective beta globin chain Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disease. There is a defect in the beta-globin chain due to the point mutation at position 6 of the beta chain which replaces glutamic acid with valine. Defective beta chains in hemoglobin make RBCs susceptible to sickling in the condition of hypoxia, dehydration and acidosis. Sickled RBCs are irregular in shape and stuck in small blood vessels resulting in vaso-occlusive crisis and hemolysis. Symptoms of sickle cell disease include pallor, jaundice, episodes of pain, swelling of hands and feet, recurrent infections, growth retardation, vision the problem, auto splenectomy (due to infarction). Sickle cell disease is also one of the causes of renal tubular acidosis type 1. Peripheral smear shows target cells and sickled RBCs. Incorrect options: Option A: Decrease synthesis of the beta-globin chain. Beta thalassemia is due to decreased production of the beta globin chain. 2 major types of beta thalassemia include: Beta thalassemia minor which is usually asymptomatic Beta thalassemia major which is symptomatic and manifest after 6 months of life. Symptoms of Beta thalassemia include fatigue, lethargy, pallor, growth retardation, recurrent infections, bony abnormalities (haemolytic facies), enlarged spleen and liver. Blood smear shows hypochromic and microcytic cells with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis Option C: Defect in the utilization of iron during erythropoiesis. Sideroblastic anemia is a type of anemia in which iron is present but iron cannot be incorporated in heme. Iron starts to accumulate inside the mitochondria of RBCs and form a ring around the nucleus such RBCs are called sideroblast. Peripheral smears show microcytic and hypochromic cells with Pappenheimer granules. Option D: Defect in membrane proteins of RBCs. Hereditary spherocytosis is a condition characterized by hemolytic anemia in which there is a defect in the RBCs membrane proteins called ankyrin, Spectrin, and band 3 proteins. Defective RBCs are susceptible to hemolysis. Symptoms include pallor, jaundice, fatigue, lethargy, gallstones, and splenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes. The Osmotic fragility test is positive. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic bronchitis visits the doctor with a 1-month history of increasing dyspnea and coughing up viscous sputum. He inhaled a single pack of cigarettes every day for 20 years before quitting 5 years ago. Vital signs are; heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30/min. Physical evaluation reveals symmetrically larger anteroposterior chest diameter and coarse crackles in the lower lung areas. The administration of a medication that effectively counteracts the effects of vagal activation on the airways is initiated. Which of the following medications was most likely initiated?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic bronchitis visits the doctor with a 1-month history of increasing dyspnea and coughing up viscous sputum. He inhaled a single pack of cigarettes every day for 20 years before quitting 5 years ago. Vital signs are; heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30/min. Physical evaluation reveals symmetrically larger anteroposterior chest diameter and coarse crackles in the lower lung areas. The administration of a medication that effectively counteracts the effects of vagal activation on the airways is initiated. Which of the following medications was most likely initiated?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Tiotropium: The antimuscarinic drug tiotropium treats asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD). This patient exhibits a persistent productive cough, a history of tobacco use, and greater anteroposterior lung girth coarse crackles on physical examination. All of these characteristics firmly point to a COPD diagnosis. Tiotropium specifically blocks the M3 muscarinic receptors in the airways, leading to the relaxation of bronchial smooth muscles and decreased bronchoconstriction. The competing binding of Tiotropium (and other long-acting parasympatholytics) to muscarinic receptors decreases the parasympathetic tone on the bronchioles, which prevents bronchoconstriction. Moreover, tiotropium also inhibits mucus secretion from goblet cells, leading to a reduction in airway obstruction. These results enhance lung efficacy and lessen the signs and symptoms of airway blockage. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fluticasone: Fluticasone and other inhaled glucocorticoids prevent the production of several cytokines, which has an anti-inflammatory impact. The transcription factor NF-B, which typically promotes the generation of inflammatory substances (such as TNF-), is inactivated by glucocorticoids in the nucleus. Despite being a component of the multimodal treatment for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inhaled glucocorticoids do not counteract the effects of vagal activation on the airways. Option C- Montelukast: Anti-inflammatory drugs called anti-leukotrienes, such as montelukast, inhibit leukotriene receptors. (CysLT1). Leukotrienes cause bronchoconstriction and lung hyperreactivity. As a result, leukotriene receptor blockade causes bronchodilation. Montelukast is not recommended to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease despite reducing lung irritation. This drug has been shown to lessen the frequency of severe asthma episodes and is frequently prescribed to manage asthma. Additionally, montelukast does not counter the impacts of vagal activation on the airways. Option D - Albuterol: Beta 2-agonist, albuterol causes bronchodilation right away. It is used to treat acute bouts of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because it is a short-acting medication; it is not a component of long-term maintenance treatment. Additionally, the impacts of vagal activation on the airways are not countered by albuterol. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old male presents with recurring episodes of wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms are only triggered in certain situations, which the patient can’t point out. He also reports coughing and difficulty breathing during exercise. His medical history is significant for eczema. On physical examination, the patient has diffuse wheezing and prolonged expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Allergic asthma: Allergic asthma is the most common form of asthma, accounting for around 50-60% of all asthma cases. It is an immunoglobulin E (Ig E)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to various allergens, including house dust mites, pollen, animal dander, and moulds. In allergic asthma, allergens are inhaled and processed by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in the airways. These APCs then present allergen peptides to T-helper 2 (Th2) cells, which produce interleukins, such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 . These interleukins activate eosinophils, which release inflammatory mediators such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins, causing bronchial smooth muscle contraction, airway oedema, and mucus production. In addition, Ig E antibodies produced by B cells in response to the allergens bind to mast cells and basophils, triggering the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators. Symptoms of allergic asthma include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, which occur in response to exposure to allergens. Incorrect Options: Option B - Occupational asthma: Occupational asthma is caused by exposure to irritants or allergens in the workplace. It is estimated to account for approximately 5-15% of adult asthma cases. While the patient's symptoms could potentially be caused by occupational asthma, the fact that she has a history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis. Option C - Exercise-induced asthma: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a type of asthma that is triggered by physical exertion. It is estimated to affect approximately 90% of individuals with asthma. However, in this scenario, the patient's symptoms are not necessarily related to physical exertion, so EIA is less likely to be the cause of her symptoms. Option D - Non-allergic asthma: Non-allergic asthma, also known as intrinsic asthma , is asthma that is not caused by an allergic response. It is estimated to account for approximately 30-40% of adult asthma cases. However, the patient's history of allergies makes allergic asthma a more likely diagnosis than non-allergic asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort. Vital capacity (VC) is the maximal volume of air that may be expelled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. A reduced FEV1/FVC is suggestive of obstructive airway disease.
